keyVerseText: And the son of an Israelitish woman, whose father was an Egyptian , went out among the children of Israel : and this son of the Israelitish woman and a man of Israel strove together in the camp;
rootMeaning: The word יִשְׂרְאֵלִית (Yisrᵉʼêlîyth) is the feminine form of יִשְׂרְאֵלִי (Yisrᵉʼêlîy), which means 'of Israel' or 'Israelite.' Rooted in the name Israel, meaning 'God prevails,' this feminine noun specifically denotes a female descendant or inhabitant of Israel. The literal sense highlights not just nationality but a connection to the covenant people of God, emphasizing identity through divine prevailing power rather than mere ethnicity.
usageInScripture: The term יִשְׂרְאֵלִית appears three times in Scripture, consistently translated as 'Israelitish' or referring to a female Israelite. Two occurrences use the gloss 'of an Israelitish,' while one instance reads 'And the Israelitish,' indicating a consistent focus on female lineage or identity within the nation of Israel. This usage underscores the importance of recognizing individual identity within the broader covenant community, especially distinguishing gender in the context of Israelite descent.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding יִשְׂרְאֵלִית enriches our grasp of covenant identity, reminding believers that God's promises encompass all descendants, including women, as integral members of His chosen people. The name Israel meaning 'God prevails' assures us that this identity is rooted in God's sovereign power and faithfulness. This word invites reflection on the inclusive nature of God's covenant and the personal belonging of each believer to God's redemptive plan. It also points forward to the New Testament reality where all who belong to Christ, male and female, share in the spiritual heritage of Israel.
keyVerseReflection: Leviticus 24:10 mentions 'the son of an Israelitish woman,' highlighting the maternal lineage within the Israelite community. This phrase stresses that the woman’s identity as an Israelite is significant even when the father was Egyptian, showing how Israelite identity was recognized through the mother in this context. The use of יִשְׂרְאֵלִית here emphasizes the inclusion and status of female Israelites and their children within the covenant people, underscoring the relational and communal aspects of Israelite identity.
